chief_complaint: recurrent kidney stones, bone pain, and high calcium
hpi_details: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with recurrent kidney stones, bone pain, and high calcium. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks her recurring kidney stones and aching bones are caused by drinking hard tap water or taking too many calcium vitamins.
concerns: She is worried that another excruciating kidney stone attack will strike right during her daughter's upcoming wedding.
expectations: She hopes to get strong pain medication to keep on hand and clear dietary guidance to prevent new stones from forming.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Primary Hyperparathyroidism is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Confirm PTH-dependent hypercalcemia and assess renal and skeletal involvement before localization studies; recurrent stones are a standard indication to refer for parathyroidectomy after diagnosis is established.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent kidney stones, bone pain, and high calcium

Key HPI features: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with recurrent kidney stones, bone pain, and high calcium. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Primary Hyperparathyroidism.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Primary Hyperparathyroidism.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: severe hypercalcaemia (>14 mg/dL) or symptoms of hypercalcaemic crisis (confusion, severe dehydration, arrhythmia), significantly elevated PTH with very high calcium, pathological fractures, significant bone loss, or nephrocalcinosis/renal impairment.
management_principles: Confirm PTH-dependent hypercalcemia, assess renal and skeletal involvement, then refer for parathyroidectomy when surgical criteria are met
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of recurrent kidney stones, bone pain, and high calcium. HPI: parathyroid adenoma.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Primary Hyperparathyroidism.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Primary Hyperparathyroidism.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm PTH-dependent hypercalcemia and assess renal and skeletal involvement. Recurrent kidney stones warrant referral for parathyroidectomy once the diagnosis is established.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Primary Hyperparathyroidism
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Primary Hyperparathyroidism
Implement evidence-based management plan: Confirm PTH-dependent hypercalcemia, assess renal and skeletal involvement, then refer for surgery when indicated

teaching.one_liner: A parathyroid adenoma causing recurrent kidney stones, bone pain, and elevated calcium.
red_flags: Severe hypercalcaemia (>14 mg/dL) or symptoms of hypercalcaemic crisis (confusion, severe dehydration, arrhythmia) — medical emergency requiring urgent treatment
Significantly elevated PTH with very high calcium — raises concern for parathyroid carcinoma rather than a benign adenoma
Pathological fractures, significant bone loss, or nephrocalcinosis/renal impairment — indicates end-organ damage and lowers the threshold for parathyroidectomy

must_ask.say: How many kidney stones have you had?
How long has this been going on?

history.answer: I have been passing kidney stones again, and lately my bones have been aching all over.
The deep bone aches and heavy tiredness started about two months ago, and they have been gradually getting worse.
The aching is mostly in my lower back, hips, and shins, without shooting down my legs.
It feels like a constant, dull, deep ache inside my bones that I would rate around a four out of ten.
The aching and fatigue have been steady and slowly worsening over the past couple of months.
Walking or standing for long periods makes the aches worse, while resting in bed takes the edge off.
Yes, I feel completely drained and exhausted all day even after a full night of sleep.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, my weight has been completely steady and my appetite is normal.
I have had two kidney stones over the past three years, with the last one passed about four months ago.
A few weeks ago, my regular doctor did blood work and told me my calcium level was abnormally high.
I tried taking over-the-counter acetaminophen for the bone aches, but it barely helped at all.
I do not take any calcium or vitamin D supplements, and I try to drink plenty of water every day.
The exhaustion and aching make it really difficult to get through my workday and manage household chores.
The ache is mainly deep inside my thighs, shins, and lower spine, with no swelling in my joints.
I have noticed some mild nausea and persistent constipation over the last month, which is unusual for me.
I have been feeling unusually irritable, down, and foggy-headed, finding it hard to concentrate.
I find myself drinking a lot more water than usual and waking up several times at night to urinate.
I feel mentally sluggish and slightly forgetful, but I have not had any severe confusion.
No, I have never broken any bones or had a fracture.
No, I have not had any headaches, vision changes, or neck stiffness.
No, my chest feels fine, with no palpitations or shortness of breath.
I wondered if the kidney stones and aching joints are because I've been taking too many over-the-counter calcium vitamins.
I'm so worried that another agonizing kidney stone will hit right in the middle of my daughter's wedding next month.
I'm hoping for a prescription for emergency pain medicine and a diet plan that stops these stones from coming back.
Aside from the two kidney stone episodes, I have had no other medical conditions or chronic illnesses.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I am not currently taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or vitamins.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink socially, having about one glass of wine on the weekend.
I work as an office administrator and live with my husband.
There is no family history of kidney stones, calcium disorders, or endocrine problems.
My periods stopped two years ago, so I have already gone through menopause.
No, there is no chance of pregnancy since I am postmenopausal.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, mildly fatigued-appearing woman in no acute distress.
Thyroid gland is normal in size and non-tender, with no palpable nodules or thyromegaly.
No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Mild diffuse tenderness on palpation over the lumbar spine without focal step-off; straight leg raise test is negative bilaterally.
Full range of motion in all peripheral joints with mild aching on palpation of the tibia and femur, without joint swelling, warmth, or erythema.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, with mild diffuse non-localized discomfort on deep palpation, and no guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal heart sounds S1 and S2, without murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Alert, oriented to person, place, and time, with mildly slowed response time but clear speech and intact cognition.
